description: A vice president of legal and supply chain must approve whether the company will invoke force majeure after a government export-control order disrupted component shipments, and must finalize the notice, insurance, and customer-continuity plan with input from contract counsel, operations, insurance counsel, and the customer-relations legal lead.

agents.name: Elena Ward
agents.role: Vice President, Legal and Supply Chain

shared_context.S1: A government export-control order has interrupted shipments of a component used in the company's industrial equipment, and several counterparties have asked for the company's contractual position.
shared_context.S2: The principal supply agreement contains a force-majeure provision, but the company has not yet sent an external notice under that provision.
shared_context.S3: Some production can continue using inventory already held at the company's facilities, although output will be materially below normal levels.
shared_context.S4: Company practice is to hold a cross-functional legal and operations review before sending a contractual disruption notice; Elena asks each participating function to report its findings and recommended action during that review.

PF1.text: While checking the executed amendment and its notice exhibit, Thomas confirmed that the government order qualifies as a force-majeure event and that notice must identify the affected facilities and be sent by both email and overnight courier within five business days. He has not circulated the confirmation because he was reconciling conflicting notice language in an older draft.

PF2.text: Mei confirmed with plant managers this morning that exactly two of the company's five facilities are affected and that the remaining facilities can produce only 40% of normal output until the order is lifted. She has not updated the legal incident file because operations is still reconciling its inventory report.

PF3.text: After reviewing the applicable supply-interruption endorsement, Samuel confirmed that the carrier must be notified within 10 calendar days and that the company must make no admission of liability in its customer communications. He has not sent a carrier notice because the claim package is awaiting the legal position on force majeure.

PF4.text: In a call with the company's largest hospital-equipment customer, Nora confirmed that preserving emergency-device deliveries is the customer's overriding priority; the agreed internal plan is to reserve exactly 60% of available output for emergency-device orders rather than suspend all shipments. She has not placed the allocation plan in the response draft because the commercial team was waiting for Elena's approval.

acceptance_conditions: The company must send a force-majeure notice.
The notice must be sent by both email and overnight courier.
The notice must identify exactly two affected facilities.
Exactly 60% of available output must be reserved for emergency-device orders.
The carrier must be notified within exactly 10 calendar days.
Customer communications must contain no admission of liability.
The settlement must include commitments to notify the carrier and implement the emergency-device allocation.

decisive_facts.why: The shared record only establishes that a force-majeure clause exists; PF1 changes the decision to send the notice and sets the exact required method as both email and overnight courier.
The shared facts do not identify the affected sites; PF2 changes the notice's facility count to exactly two.
The policy terms are not in the shared record; PF3 changes the response to a carrier notice within exactly 10 calendar days, no admission of liability, and a carrier-notice commitment.

The shared facts show reduced output but no customer allocation rule; PF4 changes the plan to reserve exactly 60% of available output for emergency-device orders and adds the matching allocation commitment.
